//areas: The unit of worker ownership. One area = one slug + the ONLY paths a worker
assigned to it may edit. Areas MUST be disjoint: `mission doctor` fails if
two areas claim the same file, because the parallelism rule assumes it.
Do NOT try to cover the whole repo. Paths owned by nobody are a feature:
they force an escalation instead of letting a path-scoped worker edit a
//surfaces: A surface is a toolchain, not a folder. Two areas share a surface when the
same commands verify them. Split when the commands differ (a server and a
mobile app usually have separate typecheck/test/lint invocations).
`designSpec: true` makes the milestone require a design spec before any UI
worker runs, and mounts it into the worker and the validator.
//gates: The milestone integration gate. This is the check that is NOT delegated and
NOT judgement-based, and it is the reason a milestone can be trusted.
Per-area tests structurally cannot see breakage that spans the repo: a type
graph, an exhaustive registry, a generated client, a cross-source consistency
suite. Every command must exit 0 before a milestone advances.
`pre` runs first — put cache-busters here. An incremental typecheck with a
warm build cache skips re-checking touched files and reports a FALSE green.
//protectedPaths: Paths a worker may never edit. Touching one is an ESCALATION: the orchestrator
either applies it inline (only for a single additive entry) or delegates it to
a dedicated worker whose output a FRESH validator reviews.
`alwaysDelegate: true` forces the delegated route regardless of size — use it
for anything whose blast radius is wide enough to want an adversarial read
`companionGlobs` are extra paths the delegated worker needs (a migrations dir
beside a schema file, a generated-types dir beside its source).
//testGlobs: Where tests live. Granted to every delegated escalation worker.
//additivePairs: Two-file shapes that count as ONE trivial additive change, so they stay
inline instead of costing a worker spawn. The classic case is an ORM schema
file plus the migration generated from it: they are inherently one change and
splitting them across seats invites drift.
//seats: Who does what. `tier` is abstract (economy | standard | frontier) and resolves
through models{} below, so the same config runs on any provider.
The validator MUST be readOnly. A validator that can edit is not a verifier:
it will quietly fix what it was asked to judge, and the verdict becomes
worthless. See docs/models.md for why the orchestrator and validator are the
//models: Tier -> concrete model id, per runtime. Leave a runtime out and the tier name
passes through literally, which is what runtimes with their own tier aliases
want. Keep this the ONLY place model ids appear, so a model upgrade is a

policy.//maxCorrectiveRounds: Two failed rounds means stuck, not unlucky. A third round reliably just burns tokens.
policy.//escalateSeatAfterRounds: Spend the frontier tier on the LAST attempt before the breaker trips, not the first.

//constraints: Project-wide rules every worker must honour, in plain language. These are
injected into every seat prompt and auto-added to the contract as default
assertions. Put the rules a newcomer would break here: logging conventions,
copy restrictions, banned imports, licence headers.
//liveGate: Optional verification that can only happen OUTSIDE the harness: a device run,
a staging deploy, a manual QA pass. The runner's exit code is the contract —
0 passes, `skipExitCode` means 'no runner available' (a SKIP, never a
regression, and never a false pass), anything else fails.
A mission with an unverified live gate is recorded `gated`, NOT `done`.
